title: Flavors of Bollywood Puts Indian Cuisine Centre Stage at New York City's Biggest Food Festival
excerpt: Chefs Maneet Chauhan and Vijay Kumar hosted a sold-out debut of street food, regional specialties and Bollywood spectacle at the NYC Wine & Food Festival, weeks ahead of Diwali.
body:
• "Flavors of Bollywood," a first-time event at the Food Network New York City Wine & Food Festival, put Indian cuisine at the centre of the city's biggest food festival on Friday, October 16, hosted by chefs Maneet Chauhan and Vijay Kumar.
  • The walk-around tasting at Storied NYC in Chelsea ran 8:00-10:30 p.m., with general admission at $195 including all food and drink; the festival's event page listed it as sold out.
  • New York City's top Indian restaurants served street food favorites, regional specialties and contemporary dishes, with unlimited cocktails, wines and spirits, live music and performances, timed weeks ahead of Diwali.
  • The wider festival ran October 15-18 in its 19th year with more than 50 events; net proceeds support the Event Zero Foundation and the James Beard Foundation.

Indian food took a headline slot at New York City's biggest food festival this week. "Flavors of Bollywood," a new event at the Food Network New York City Wine & Food Festival presented by Invesco QQQ, brought together the city's top Indian restaurants on Friday, October 16 for an evening built around India's regional cuisines and the music and glamour of its film industry, according to the festival's announcement. The festival, in its 19th year, ran October 15-18 with more than 50 events across the city.

A sold-out night in Chelsea

The event ran from 8:00 p.m. to 10:30 p.m. at Storied NYC, 547 West 26th Street in Chelsea, as a walk-around tasting for guests aged 21 and over. General admission was $195, inclusive of food, drink, taxes and ticketing fees, and the festival's event page listed tickets as sold out. Participating restaurants served street food favorites, regional specialties and contemporary dishes, paired with unlimited cocktails, wines and spirits, with music, entertainment and performances running through the evening. Anu Sehgal of The Culture Tree helped bring the cultural elements of the celebration to life.

Two chefs, two very different Indias

The hosts span the range of Indian cooking in America. Maneet Chauhan, a James Beard Award-winning chef and Food Network's "Chopped" judge, is a team captain on "BBQ Brawl" and a two-time "Tournament of Champions" winner; she runs Chauhan Ale & Masala House in Nashville and eet by Maneet Chauhan at Disney Springs. Vijay Kumar, chef of Semma in the West Village, won the James Beard Award for Best Chef: New York State for his village-style Tamil cooking; Semma holds a Michelin star and topped The New York Times list of the city's 100 best restaurants in 2025. Between them, the two presented Indian cuisine as both televised spectacle and regional tradition rooted in specific places: Chauhan's pan-Indian restaurant cooking and Kumar's food from his home district of Dindigul in Tamil Nadu.

Timed for Diwali

The festival scheduled the event with Diwali, the Festival of Lights, a few weeks away, framing the night as a season opener for the holiday. The format leaned into that: Bollywood-inspired music and performance alongside the food, and a menu that ranged across regions rather than defaulting to the standard North Indian restaurant canon. For New York's Indian-American audience, it was a mainstream festival stage, not a community hall: the event sat in the same Friday lineup as "Best of the Best," which showcased more than 15 James Beard Award winners, nominees and semifinalists.

Part of a four-day citywide program

The festival opened Thursday, October 15 with the Blue Moon Burger Bash hosted by Rachael Ray and Bert Kreischer at The Rooftop at Pier 17, and closed Sunday, October 18 with The Cookout hosted by JJ Johnson and Angela Yee, featuring a performance by Method Man and an appearance by Whoopi Goldberg. Saturday's program included New York After Dark hosted by Kwame Onwuachi. Over 18 years, the festival has generated more than $15 million in net proceeds for its charitable causes; this year's proceeds support the Event Zero Foundation and the James Beard Foundation. Within that program, "Flavors of Bollywood" was the festival's clearest statement yet that Indian cuisine belongs in its top tier, with a debut that sold out.
